opus-5.5.text:
I think proofs are a really useful starting point, partly because they're the one case where we have a very clear notion of what it means to explain why something is true. If you have a proof that a network has some property, you understand in a pretty strong sense why it has that property. So when I'm trying to say what I want out of interpretability, "something like a proof" is a natural anchor.

But I don't think proofs are quite the right picture, for a few reasons. The main one is that most of the behaviors we care about in neural networks aren't things that are actually provable. If you look at why a model predicts the next token correctly on some input, it's usually not that there's a crisp logical guarantee. It's more like there are a bunch of features that are correlated in the training distribution, and they add up in a way that tends to give the right answer, and there's a lot of noise that mostly cancels out. If you demanded a proof, you'd have to handle every weird worst-case interaction, and that's just not how the network works. It's not why the behavior happens.

So the thing we've been thinking about at ARC is more like heuristic arguments, or what you might call probabilistic or defeasible reasoning. The analogy I like is how mathematicians reason about things like the twin prime conjecture. Nobody has a proof, but there's a very convincing heuristic argument: you treat the primes as if they're sort of random with the right density, you compute what you'd expect, and you get an answer that matches the data extremely well. That's an explanation. It tells you why you see what you see, even though it isn't a proof, and it could in principle be overturned if you discovered some structure you hadn't accounted for.

I think explanations of neural network behavior are going to look much more like that. You say, "here are the mechanisms that are doing the work, and I'm going to treat everything else as noise that's independent of what I care about," and then you check whether that accounts for the behavior. The hard part, and the part we spend a lot of time on, is formalizing what counts as a good heuristic argument, because unlike proofs we don't have a clean definition. You want something that has the nice properties of proofs, that it's checkable, that it actually captures the reason, without requiring this impossible level of certainty.

So: proofs are a great source of intuition and a good sanity check, like "would this be satisfying if it were a proof?", but I expect the actual object we want is looser and more statistical than that.

r001.rationale: The response says most neural network behaviors are not provable and describes them as noisy, statistical interactions, contrasting that with proof-based analysis.

r002.rationale: It calls proofs a useful starting point and a natural anchor for interpretability because they offer a clear account of why something is true, while qualifying that the actual explanations will be looser.

fable-5.1.text:
I think proofs are a useful starting point, but mostly as a kind of limiting case that you then have to relax. The thing I like about proofs is that they give you a clear standard for what it means to have actually explained something. If I claim a network does X because of Y, a proof says exactly what that claim commits me to, and there's no room for me to fool myself about whether the explanation actually accounts for the behavior. That's the property I care most about, and it's the property that most informal interpretability work lacks.

The problem is that for the actual behaviors we care about, proofs are almost certainly not available. If you take a trained model and ask "why does it output this token," the real answer involves a huge number of weak correlations and heuristics that each contribute a little bit. A proof would have to track all of those, and the proof would end up being roughly as large as the model itself, if it exists at all. So if you insist on the full rigor of a proof, you get nothing.

So the way I think about it is: what's the thing that's proof-like in the sense of being precise and checkable, but that degrades gracefully? A proof is a way of establishing that some statement holds with certainty. What we probably want instead is a way of establishing that some statement holds with high probability, or on average, and where the explanation itself does the work of justifying that estimate. You want something where the explanation is responsible for making predictions about the model's behavior, and you can check those predictions, and when the explanation is incomplete you lose some accuracy rather than losing everything.

That's basically the motivation for the heuristic arguments work. You start from the picture of a proof, you notice that the thing that makes proofs valuable is that they let you verify claims without having to just run the system and look, and then you ask what the weakest structure is that still gives you that property. And I think the answer looks like something where you're reasoning about the distribution of activations, tracking which correlations you've accounted for, and treating everything else as if it were independent. That's not a proof, and it can be wrong, but it's rigorous in the sense that it's clear what it's claiming and clear what it would mean for it to fail.

So useful as a picture of the standard, not very useful as a picture of the artifact you'll actually produce.

r001.rationale: The response says proofs are almost certainly unavailable for the behaviors of interest and that a full proof could be as large as the model, while practical analysis must use weaker, probabilistic explanations.

r002.rationale: It endorses proofs as a useful starting point and standard for what a precise explanation should achieve, while qualifying them as a limiting case rather than the artifact one would produce.

astra-6.text:
I think proofs are a useful mental picture, although they can also be misleading. The useful part is that you can have an argument that’s much easier to check than it was to discover. You might need a very smart system to figure out why a neural network behaves a certain way, but you’d like the resulting explanation to be something you can scrutinize without trusting that system.

The part I’m less sure about is whether we should expect explanations to look like mathematical proofs. If you ask why a model gives a particular answer, there may be an enormous number of details that matter, and an explanation that follows all of them could be roughly as complicated as running the model. What you usually want is something more selective: which features of the computation are responsible for the behavior you care about?

So I’m more excited about an explanation of why the model won’t do some particular bad thing than a complete explanation of everything the model does. And even there, the argument might depend on empirical claims or approximations. The analogy to proofs is helpful for thinking about checking an argument, but it doesn’t by itself tell us what kinds of arguments will exist or whether they’ll be short enough to be useful.

r001.rationale: The response notes that explanations may be complex and that the proof analogy has limits, but it does not identify a large gap between what can be proved and how a neural network would be analyzed.

r002.rationale: It calls proofs a useful mental picture, but does not tentatively endorse them as the best available picture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think proofs are a useful mental picture, although I don’t expect an explanation of a neural network to look like a conventional mathematical proof. The thing I like about proofs is that you can check a complicated argument without having to be as clever as the person who came up with it. You break it into steps, and each step is something you can understand and verify.

You could imagine doing something similar with a neural network. The network does some complicated computation, and you want an explanation of why that computation has a particular property. Ideally, checking that explanation would be much easier than discovering it yourself.

The hard part is figuring out what property you actually want to establish. “This network always does the right thing” isn’t a very well-defined mathematical statement. And if you prove something about a simplified model, you still have to ask whether that captures what you cared about in the actual system. So proofs give me a useful picture of how verification could work, but they don’t by themselves solve the problem of what an adequate explanation would be.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes proof checking from explaining a network: choosing a meaningful property is hard, and results on simplified models may not apply to the actual system. It concludes that proofs alone do not provide an adequate explanation.

r002.rationale: The response calls proofs a useful mental picture, but does not endorse them as the best available picture.
